title: Stack with Vec
story: You're writing a parser that needs to match brackets. Every time you see `(`, you push. Every time you see `)`, you pop. If the stack is empty when you need to pop, the brackets are unbalanced. This is the classic stack problem — and you're going to build the stack yourself.
why: Stacks model undo/redo, function call history, bracket matching, and depth-first search — the LIFO pattern is everywhere, and building one manually teaches you fundamental data structure operations.
analogy: A stack is like a stack of cafeteria trays — you can only take the top tray (pop) or add a new one on top (push). You can't pull a tray from the middle, and you can't add one to the bottom. The spring-loaded dispenser ensures Last In, First Out.
try_it: Build a `reverse_string` function using a stack: push each character, then pop them all — they come out in reverse order. Then build the balanced parentheses checker from the narrative. Extend it to handle `[]` and `{}` too — push when you see an opener, check that the closer matches the top of the stack before popping.
tips: Stack uses Vec.pop() which already returns Option[T] — the stack's pop is just a wrapper
Push = add to end (top), Pop = remove from end (top) — both are O(1) with Vec
The balanced parentheses algorithm is the classic stack interview question — know it well
common_mistakes: Confusing stack (LIFO) with queue (FIFO) — stack pops the MOST RECENT item, queue pops the OLDEST
Using push/pop without checking emptiness — popping an empty stack returns None, handle it
Forgetting to match on Option when using pop/peek — these return Option[T], not T directly
